enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves in a plane so that, at time $t$ seconds, its polar coordinates relative to a fixed origin $O$ are $r = 3t$ metres and $\theta = t^{2}$ radians. The transverse component of the acceleration of $P$ when $t = 3$, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In polar coordinates the acceleration has radial component $a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}$ and transverse component $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. Differentiate $r$ and $\theta$ with respect to $t$ first, then substitute the given value of $t$.

### Solution

$r=3t$ gives $\dot r=3$ and $\ddot r=0$; $\theta=t^{2}$ gives $\dot\theta=2t$ and $\ddot\theta=2$.

At $t=3$: $r=9$, $\dot r=3$, $\dot\theta=6$, $\ddot\theta=2$. Then

$$a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=9(2)+2(3)(6)=18+36=54\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

**Answer: c.** The value $18$ forgets the term $2\dot r\dot\theta$, $36$ keeps only that term, and $72$ uses $\theta=9$ instead of $\dot\theta=6$ in it.

enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves on the curve with polar equation $r = a\,e^{\theta}$, where $a$ is a positive constant, with constant angular speed $\omega$. The radial and transverse components $(a_r,\ a_\theta)$ of the acceleration of $P$ are
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use $a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}$ and $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. When the angular speed is constant, $\dot\theta=\omega$ and $\ddot\theta=0$, so the only work is to differentiate $r$ twice with the chain rule.

### Solution

$\dot r=a e^{\theta}\dot\theta=r\omega$, and, since $\omega$ is constant, $\ddot r=\dot r\,\omega=r\omega^{2}$.

$$a_r=\ddot r-r\omega^{2}=r\omega^{2}-r\omega^{2}=0,\qquad a_\theta=r(0)+2(r\omega)\omega=2r\omega^{2}.$$

**Answer: d.** Option a is the result for motion on a circle ($\dot r=0$). Option b forgets the factor $2$. Option c forgets to subtract $r\dot\theta^{2}$ from $\ddot r$.

enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves on a circle of radius $0.5\ \mathrm m$ whose centre is the origin $O$. At a certain instant the angular speed of $P$ about $O$ is $4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and this angular speed is increasing at the rate of $6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}$.

Find, at this instant,

(i) the components of the acceleration of $P$ along $OP$ (outwards) and perpendicular to $OP$ (in the sense of increasing $\theta$),

(ii) the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$,

(iii) the angle between the acceleration of $P$ and the direction $PO$. *[6 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On a circle $r$ is constant, so $\dot r=\ddot r=0$ and the general formulas reduce to $a_r=-r\dot\theta^{2}$ (towards the centre) and $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta$. The components are perpendicular, so the magnitude follows from Pythagoras and the angle from a tangent ratio.

### Solution

**(i)** With $r=0.5$, $\dot\theta=4$, $\ddot\theta=6$:

$$a_r=-r\dot\theta^{2}=-0.5(16)=-8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\qquad a_\theta=r\ddot\theta=0.5(6)=3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

The radial component is directed towards $O$ (the sign is negative because $\mathbf e_r$ points away from $O$).

**(ii)** $$|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{8^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{73}\approx 8.54\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

**(iii)** $\overrightarrow{PO}$ is the direction of the $8$ component, so the angle $\phi$ satisfies

$$\tan\phi=\frac{3}{8}\ \Rightarrow\ \phi\approx 20.6^{\circ}.$$

enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves on the spiral $r = 0.4\,\theta$, where $r$ is in metres and $\theta$ in radians, with constant angular speed $3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. When $\theta = 2.5$, the transverse component of the acceleration of $P$, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Because $\dot\theta$ is constant, $\ddot\theta=0$ and $a_\theta=2\dot r\dot\theta$. The derivative $\dot r$ needs the chain rule: $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\,\dot\theta$.

### Solution

$$\dot r=0.4\,\dot\theta=0.4(3)=1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=0+2(1.2)(3)=7.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

The value of $\theta$ is not needed for the transverse component. **Answer: c.** The value $2.4$ takes $\dot r=0.4$ (no chain rule), $3.6$ forgets the factor $2$, and $9.0$ is $|a_r|=r\dot\theta^{2}=(1.0)(9)$, the radial component.

enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves in a plane so that the transverse component of its acceleration is zero at every instant. When its distance from the origin $O$ is $4\ \mathrm m$, its angular speed about $O$ is $1.5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. When $P$ is $6\ \mathrm m$ from $O$, its angular speed about $O$ is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The transverse acceleration can be written $a_\theta=\dfrac1r\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(r^{2}\dot\theta\right)$. If it is always zero, then $r^{2}\dot\theta$ is constant (conservation of angular momentum per unit mass).

### Solution

$$r^{2}\dot\theta=4^{2}(1.5)=24=6^{2}\dot\theta_{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \dot\theta_{2}=\frac{24}{36}=\frac23\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.$$

**Answer: a.** Option b wrongly keeps $r\dot\theta$ constant, option c makes $\dot\theta$ proportional to $r$, and option d makes it proportional to $r^{2}$.

enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ moves in a plane so that its polar coordinates at time $t$ seconds are
$$r = 0.5\,(1+\sin\theta)\ \text{metres},\qquad \theta = 2t\ \text{radians}.$$

(i) Show that the acceleration of $P$ has components $-2(1+2\sin\theta)$ along $OP$ and $4\cos\theta$ perpendicular to $OP$ (in the sense of increasing $\theta$), in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(ii) Find the values of $\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ for which the acceleration of $P$ is purely transverse, and the magnitude of the acceleration at these instants.

(iii) Show that the magnitude of the acceleration is $2\sqrt{5+4\sin\theta}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and deduce its greatest value. *[10 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

With $\dot\theta=\omega$ constant, $a_r=\ddot r-r\omega^{2}$ and $a_\theta=2\dot r\omega$. Differentiate $r$ with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, then use $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ to combine the two perpendicular components.

### Solution

**(i)** $\dot\theta=2$, $\ddot\theta=0$. With $r=0.5(1+\sin\theta)$:

$$\dot r=0.5\cos\theta\,\dot\theta=\cos\theta,\qquad \ddot r=-\sin\theta\,\dot\theta=-2\sin\theta.$$

$$a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}=-2\sin\theta-2(1+\sin\theta)=-2(1+2\sin\theta),$$

$$a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=0+2\cos\theta(2)=4\cos\theta.$$

**(ii)** The acceleration is purely transverse when $a_r=0$, that is $\sin\theta=-\tfrac12$. In $[0,2\pi)$ this gives $\theta=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ or $\theta=\dfrac{11\pi}{6}$. There $\cos\theta=\mp\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, so

$$|\mathbf a|=|a_\theta|=4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=2\sqrt3\approx 3.46\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

**(iii)** The components are perpendicular:

$$|\mathbf a|^{2}=4(1+2\sin\theta)^{2}+16\cos^{2}\theta=4\left(1+4\sin\theta+4\sin^{2}\theta+4\cos^{2}\theta\right)=4(5+4\sin\theta).$$

Hence $|\mathbf a|=2\sqrt{5+4\sin\theta}$. This is greatest when $\sin\theta=1$ (that is $\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$), giving $|\mathbf a|_{\max}=2\sqrt9=6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
